title: Linux Fundamentals II: permissions, users and processes
description: Understand rwx and SUID bits, who runs the system, and how to inspect processes: the foundation of privilege escalation.

1.title: Reading permissions like a professional
1.body:
## Anatomy of an ls -l

```text
-rwxr-x--- 1 ana dev 2048 nov 1 12:00 script.sh
│└┬┘└┬┘└┬┘     └─ group
│ │  │  └── others (the rest of the world)
│ │  └───── group (dev)
│ └──────── owner (ana)
└────────── type: - file, d directory, l link
```

Each trio adds up with **r=4, w=2, x=1**:

- `rwx` = 7 · `r-x` = 5 · `r--` = 4 · `---` = 0
- That's why `chmod 754 script.sh` leaves the file exactly as `rwxr-xr--`.

On **directories**, `x` doesn't mean "execute" but **being able to enter** (cd). A directory
with `r` but no `x` lists names but doesn't let you access them.

## Changing permissions and owners

```bash
chmod u+x script.sh        # symbolic: u/g/o/a + - r/w/x
chmod 754 script.sh        # octal: owner-group-others
chown ana:dev script.sh    # change owner and group (requires privileges)
```

`sudo` runs things as root: `sudo chown root:root fichero`. Use it with respect, and check
`sudo -l` (what can I do as root?) — a CTF enumeration classic.

linux-fundamentos-2-t01-q01.prompt: In '-rwxr-x---', what does the second trio (r-x) mean, and for whom?
linux-fundamentos-2-t01-q01.hint: owner, group, others — in that order.

options.a: The owner can read and write
options.b: The group can read and execute, but not write

linux-fundamentos-2-t01-q02.prompt: Which command (symbolic mode) ADDS execute permission ONLY for the owner of a file? Give the exact command for script.sh.

linux-fundamentos-2-t01-q03.prompt: Which octal value equals rwxr-xr-- (owner everything, group read+execute, others read only)?
linux-fundamentos-2-t01-q03.hint: r=4, w=2, x=1. Add up each trio: 7, 5 and…

2.title: Users, groups and the SUID bit
2.body:
## Where users live

```bash
cat /etc/passwd    # users: name:x:uid:gid:home:shell
cat /etc/group     # groups
cat /etc/shadow    # password hashes (only root can read it!)
id                 # who am I: uid, gid and groups
sudo -l            # which commands I can run as root
```

In `/etc/passwd`, the `x` field points to `/etc/shadow`. If some service writes
users by hand and forgets that `x` (leaving the hash in plain sight), you already have a
problem — you'll see it in future labs.

## SUID: the bit that grants powers

When the **SUID** bit is set, the binary runs with its **owner's** permissions.
That's why `/usr/bin/passwd` can edit `/etc/shadow` even when a regular user runs it:

```bash
ls -l /usr/bin/passwd
# -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ... /usr/bin/passwd
#     ↑ the 's' where the owner's x would be = SUID
```

To find SUID binaries across a whole machine (classic privesc enumeration):

```bash
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
```

The security question is always: is there any **writable** SUID binary or any "abusable"
binary (look it up on GTFOBins)? The first case is direct escalation.

linux-fundamentos-2-t02-q01.prompt: Which plain-text file lists the system's local users?
linux-fundamentos-2-t02-q01.hint: Each user is one line with 7 fields delimited by :

linux-fundamentos-2-t02-q02.prompt: Which special bit makes a binary run with its OWNER's permissions (e.g. root) even when another user launches it?
linux-fundamentos-2-t02-q02.hint: The s that shows up where the owner's x would be.

linux-fundamentos-2-t02-q03.prompt: A binary -rwsr-xr-x root root is SUID root and writable by anyone. What is the risk?

options.a: None: SUID only affects the access date
options.b: Immediate escalation: anyone can replace the binary and root will run it

3.title: Processes and services
3.body:
## Everything that runs is a process

```bash
ps aux                     # all processes, with their user
ps aux | grep sshd         # is ssh running?
top / htop                 # live processes (CPU, memory)
kill <PID>                 # SIGTERM: "please, terminate"
kill -9 <PID>              # SIGKILL: immediate death, no cleanup
```

Every process has an owner. Seeing a process running as **root** that shouldn't be
(your app, a script) is gold for an attacker — and an alert for a defender.

## Services with systemd

```bash
systemctl status nginx     # status of a service
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
journalctl -u nginx -f     # the service's logs, live
```

Services (daemons, names ending in `d`: `sshd`, `systemd-resolved`) usually
start with the system and run as root or under dedicated accounts (`www-data`).

## Express enumeration of a machine

When you compromise a Linux machine, this will be your first round:

```bash
whoami && id               # who am I
sudo -l                    # what can I escalate
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null   # SUID
ps aux | head -20          # what is running and AS whom
cat /etc/crontab           # scheduled tasks
```

Save these commands: you'll repeat this list in every lab of the path. You've finished
the Linux basics — in the next modules you'll use them to attack for real.

linux-fundamentos-2-t03-q01.prompt: Which command lists every process on the system along with its user (classic BSD syntax)?
linux-fundamentos-2-t03-q01.hint: Two letters plus options; we showed it to you filtering nginx with grep.

linux-fundamentos-2-t03-q02.prompt: Which signal does 'kill -9' send to a process?
linux-fundamentos-2-t03-q02.hint: The one that can't be caught or ignored.

linux-fundamentos-2-t03-q03.prompt: Which command manages services on a modern systemd system (just one)?
linux-fundamentos-2-t03-q03.hint: The 'control' in systemctl… is the command itself.

4.title: Lab: permissions and processes on a real system
4.body:
## Practice in the lab

### Exercise 1: searching logs
```bash
grep -r "secret" /var/log/        # recursive: searches every file
```

### Exercise 2: group permissions
```bash
id                                 # check that you're in the flagreaders group
find / -name "*flag*" 2>/dev/null # find the files with flag in their name
ls -la /opt/group_only_flag.txt    # look at the permissions: r--r-----
cat /opt/group_only_flag.txt       # you can read it because you're in the group
```

The lesson: Unix permissions aren't just rwx for the owner — the group AND others matter.

linux-fundamentos-2-t04-q01.prompt: Find the flag in an application log (use a recursive grep).

linux-fundamentos-2-t04-q02.prompt: Read the flag in a file that only the 'flagreaders' group can see (you're already a member).
